canonical_statement: The 26th Amendment says citizens 18 and older can vote — one of four voting-rights amendments.
linked_questions: There are four amendments to the U.S. Constitution about who can vote. Describe one of them.
accepted_answer_variants: You don't have to pay (a poll tax) to vote.
Any citizen can vote. (Women and men can vote.)
A male citizen of any race (can vote).
curation_rationale: Most directly relevant to the reader's own situation (a future voter), and pairs naturally with the four-amendment set already scattered elsewhere (15th, 19th, 24th, 26th).

canonical_statement: Only U.S. citizens can vote in federal elections, run for federal office, and serve on a jury.
linked_questions: Who can vote in federal elections, run for federal office, and serve on a jury in the United States?

canonical_statement: Freedom of speech, freedom of religion, and the right to bear arms are three rights of everyone living in the United States.
linked_questions: What are three rights of everyone living in the United States?
curated_answer: Freedom of speech, freedom of religion, the right to bear arms
curation_rationale: Three of the most distinct and widely recognized rights from the six accepted options, deliberately varied rather than picking three near-synonyms (e.g. speech/expression/petition all overlap conceptually).
visual_treatment: Three-icon row, matching the existing icon_set pattern used for national holidays.

canonical_statement: The Pledge of Allegiance shows loyalty to the United States and the flag.
linked_questions: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
curated_answer: The United States and the flag
curation_rationale: Both accepted answers given together — they're not really alternatives, they're the same idea from two angles.

canonical_statement: New citizens promise to defend the Constitution and obey the laws of the United States.
linked_questions: Name two promises that new citizens make in the Oath of Allegiance.
accepted_answer_variants: Give up loyalty to other countries
Obey the laws of the United States
Be loyal to the United States
curated_answer: Defend the Constitution and obey the laws
curation_rationale: The two most concrete, action-oriented promises of the five accepted options — easier to picture than the more abstract 'give up loyalty' or 'be loyal' phrasings.
visual_treatment: Balance scale — law and constitutional loyalty both fit the justice-symbol family already established.

canonical_statement: People can become U.S. citizens by being born in the U.S., naturalizing, or deriving citizenship through parents.
linked_questions: How can people become United States citizens?
accepted_answer_variants: Be born in the United States
Derive citizenship (under conditions set by Congress)
curation_rationale: Chosen specifically because it's the reader's own path — the most personally relevant of the three, not just the most common one.
visual_treatment: Seal icon — a formal, official process.

canonical_statement: Voting and joining a political party are two examples of civic participation.
linked_questions: What are two examples of civic participation in the United States?
curated_answer: Vote and join a political party
curation_rationale: The two most concrete, familiar actions among six options.

canonical_statement: Paying taxes is one way Americans can serve their country.
linked_questions: What is one way Americans can serve their country?
curation_rationale: Chosen deliberately to set up fact 71 (why paying taxes matters) as a natural two-page sequence rather than picking an unrelated answer like 'vote', which is already well covered elsewhere in the book.

canonical_statement: Paying federal taxes is required by the 16th Amendment and is a civic duty.
linked_questions: Why is it important to pay federal taxes?
accepted_answer_variants: All people pay to fund the federal government
curation_rationale: Most specific and memorable of the accepted answers — a named amendment beats a vague 'civic duty'.
visual_treatment: Same dollar-bill icon as fact 70 — deliberate pairing.

canonical_statement: Men age 18 through 25 must register for the Selective Service because it's required by law.
linked_questions: It is important for all men age 18 through 25 to register for the Selective Service. Name one reason why.
accepted_answer_variants: Makes the draft fair, if needed
curation_rationale: Most direct of the three accepted answers.
visual_treatment: Age-range badge, distinct from fact 63's '18+' badge — different thresholds, deliberately different visuals.
